passages.title: Paper
passages.text: This paper presents a full vision-guided Connect-4 robot that couples board-state extraction, trusted-state validation, minimax move planning, physical token dispensing, and post-move camera verification. An overhead Raspberry Pi camera module observes the board while a Raspberry Pi 4 [1] runs a Python/OpenCV [2] pipeline that localizes the blue frame, warps the board to an 800×800 view, conditions the image, and classifies each cell in one of three modes: HSV, Auto, or ML. The accepted state is passed through a six-rule validator before a depth-5 minimax solver selects the robot move.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The target column is then sent at 9600 baud to an Arduino-controlled carriage and magazine mechanism, and the camera re-reads the board to confirm that the expected token actually appeared. Across approximately 200 labeled cell ROIs in the final evaluation set, HSV achieved 98% per-cell accuracy, Auto achieved 96%, and ML achieved 91%, making HSV the strongest practical mode under the tested indoor setup. The drop mechanism achieved 95% overall success, with 100% success in columns 1–3 and 85% in column 7, showing that open-loop carriage travel, not segmentation, was the dominant physical bottleneck.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The reported end-to-end cycle averaged 7.5 s, and the final course test suite recorded 31/31 passed core logic checks. These results document representative end-to-end closed-loop demonstrations backed by separate logic-layer validation, while remaining limited by lighting shift, domain shift, and dispenser mechanics.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Autonomous board-game robots are useful mechatronic benchmarks because they force perception, reasoning, and actuation to agree on the same physical state in real time [3]. A Connect-4 robot must read the board, infer the next legal move, position a dispenser over the chosen column, and verify that the physical outcome matches the internal plan. The challenge is not only to solve each stage independently, but to prevent small perception or actuation errors from silently corrupting the game state. Prior work has treated the main subproblems separately. Vision papers show that canonical board rectification and per-cell inference are effective for structured tabletop games [4], [5].

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: HSV-based color segmentation remains attractive in robotic handling when illumination is reasonably controlled and the target colors are well separated [6]. Chess-playing robots also show that robust physical manipulation of game pieces is often harder than the game reasoning itself [7]. Connect-4 simplifies the manipulator geometry because only lateral positioning is needed, but it still requires robust token-color recognition and gravity-aware validation. The gap addressed in this project is the lack of a tightly documented end-to-end Connect-4 implementation in which camera-based perception, trusted board-state acceptance, physical token placement, and post-move re-verification are all treated as one closed loop.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: For course deliverables, it is easy to report a working classifier, a working minimax solver, or a working dispenser separately. The harder and more important question is whether the complete system keeps a trustworthy state when the real hardware misses, stalls, or sees ambiguous frames. This paper makes four concrete contributions. It documents a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which a trusted-state validator gates the board before action and a camera re-check gates the board after action. It benchmarks three perception modes – HSV, Auto, and ML – and shows that HSV is the strongest practical operating mode under the tested indoor conditions.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: It shows that the dominant real-world bottleneck is mechanical drop reliability, especially for long carriage travel toward the edge columns, rather than image segmentation accuracy. It reports representative end-to-end demonstrations with honest limits: the integrated robot closes the loop in the archived demos, while the separate 31/31 logic checks show that the state machine remained stable before hardware uncertainty entered the loop. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the most relevant literature and motivates the system boundary used here. Section III summarizes the integrated architecture and the final physical setup.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Section IV explains the vision and state-estimation pipeline and compares the three classifier modes. Section V describes trusted-state validation, move planning, and post-drop verification. Section VI interprets the final experimental results. Section VII discusses the main lessons and limitations. Section VIII concludes.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Wolflein and Arandjelovic decomposed chess-state extraction into board localization, homographic rectification, and square-level recognition [4]. That decomposition transfers well to Connect-4 because the board is still a fixed grid, but the classifier changes from piece identity to three states: empty, red, and yellow. Masouris and van Gemert later showed that end-to-end learning can reduce hand-crafted geometry stages at the cost of a larger training burden [5]. For a course project with modest data, the modular route is more practical because each failure can be inspected directly.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: II-B. Color Segmentation Under Lighting Variation
passages.text: Akış and Dişlitaş showed that HSV-based object detection remains strong in robotic handling when color is the dominant cue and lighting is managed carefully [6]. Their findings match the Connect-4 setting: token hue is informative, while raw RGB intensity alone is less stable. The same literature also warns that fixed thresholds weaken under large lighting shifts, which matters here because the board and tokens are glossy plastic surfaces.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: II-C. Game Robots and Embedded Decision Layers
passages.text: Board-game robots such as Gambit show that unconstrained manipulation of pieces, not game reasoning, is often the harder part of the problem [7]. On the decision side, depth-limited minimax with alpha-beta pruning remains a practical baseline for Connect-4 because the game is structured, discrete, and fully observable [8]. The missing piece is the interface between these subsystems: a robot still needs a trusted physical board state before the search is meaningful, and a verified post-move state before the next turn is safe.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Figure 1 summarizes the system as a closed loop with two state gates. The first gate is trusted-state validation before planning. The second gate is post-drop camera verification before the internal state advances to the next turn. The final setup used a Raspberry Pi 4 [1] for perception and planning, an Arduino Uno [9] for motor control, an overhead Raspberry Pi camera module, a time-based lateral carriage, and an encoder-coupled magazine release. The final as-built hardware cost reported in the course materials was 6100 EGP. The operator dashboard ran on the Pi and exposed the raw feed, the warped feed, board-state views, classifier mode selection, and robot status.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The perception stack starts from a single overhead board image and converts it into a board state that the robot can trust enough to plan from. The board is first localized from the blue frame, then rectified to a canonical top-down view using the homography in (1) After warping, the deployed runtime applies a brightness shift of c=+20, a contrast gain of α=1.3, and a 5×5 Gaussian blur before partitioning the board into a 6×7 lattice. These are the values in the deployed runtime included with the repository; the final course report lists an earlier operating point of c=+30 and α=1.4.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Figure 3 gives the curated pipeline story for one representative board. Each panel answers a different question: whether the raw scene is readable, whether geometry has been normalized, whether token positions are interpreted correctly, and whether the result is usable as a state matrix. The system exposes three classifier modes. HSV: rule-based token classification using calibrated red and yellow HSV ranges. ML: a RandomForest classifier trained on compact color-statistics features extracted from cell regions. Auto: a hybrid mode that prefers the ML prediction when its confidence exceeds 0.65 and otherwise falls back to HSV.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Table I reports the final per-cell comparison across approximately 200 labeled cell ROIs captured under the deployment lighting. The table is useful not just because it ranks the modes, but because it shows where the weaker modes fail: the ML path drops most sharply on yellow cells, and the hybrid mode inherits some of that penalty even though it has access to the HSV fallback.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Table I, per-cell classification accuracy by operating mode. HSV: 99% empty, 98% red, 98% yellow, 98% overall. Auto: 97% empty, 95% red, 96% yellow, 96% overall. ML: 94% empty, 92% red, 88% yellow, 91% overall.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The board extracted from vision is not accepted blindly. Instead, it is compared against the last trusted board and must satisfy six rules before planning begins: the board must have changed, no chip may disappear, exactly one new chip may appear, the new chip must respect gravity, the target column must not already be full, and the new chip color must match the current turn. These checks are what keep imperfect frame-by-frame perception from becoming a corrupted game state. Once a candidate board passes validation, the robot chooses a move using the depth-5 minimax recursion in (2) with alpha-beta pruning,

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: where A(S) is the set of legal columns and T(S,a) is the gravity-respecting state transition induced by dropping a token in column a. The archived runtime also includes immediate-win and immediate-block shortcuts before the full search, which matters because the robot only needs a good move quickly, not a mathematically exhaustive search of every future board. The chosen column is transmitted at 9600 baud to the Arduino. The carriage first moves laterally using calibrated durations [0, 330, 600, 900, 1200, 1500, 1800] ms for columns 1 through 7 and holds 2 s over the target; the magazine motor then rotates 430 encoder pulses with a fast/slow two-stage profile to release one token, and 0.5 s later the carriage returns home.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: After a 2.5 s settling delay, the camera polls the board every 0.4 s until 10 s after the command. The internal state advances only if the expected new token is observed in the commanded column.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: VI-A. Why HSV Is the Practical Default
passages.text: Table I shows that HSV reached 98% overall per-cell accuracy, ahead of Auto at 96% and ML at 91%. The number matters because it establishes the deployed operating point: under the tested indoor setup, the simplest classifier was also the best one. The reason is visible in the project conditions and code structure. The board frame and tokens occupy distinct hue ranges, while the ML path was trained on a much smaller labeled set and had to generalize from compact color-statistics features. In practice, that left the learned model more exposed to lighting and appearance variation, especially for yellow cells.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: VI-A. Why HSV Is the Practical Default
passages.text: The Auto mode is still useful because it demonstrates an integrated bonus path rather than a disconnected side experiment, but its lower score shows that adding a learned branch is not automatically an upgrade. In this system, the hybrid only becomes meaningfully attractive if a larger and more diverse labeled dataset is collected.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: VI-B. Mechanical Drop Reliability Dominates the Real Bottleneck
passages.text: Figure 4 reports the final token-drop success rates over 20 trials per column. Columns 1–3 achieved 100% success, columns 4 and 5 achieved 95%, column 6 achieved 90%, and column 7 dropped to 85%. The overall success rate was 95% across 140 drops. These numbers matter because they change the diagnosis of the system. The robot already sees the board well enough for play; what it does not yet do equally well is deliver the physical token to every column with the same repeatability. The reason is the time-based carriage.

passages.title: Paper
passages.section: VI-B. Mechanical Drop Reliability Dominates the Real Bottleneck
passages.text: Travel error accumulates as the commanded distance grows, so the edge columns are more exposed than the center columns. Once the carriage is correctly aligned, the encoder-coupled magazine release is much more repeatable than the carriage itself. That is why the main reliability curve is indexed by column distance rather than by token color or board occupancy.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The final materials reported an end-to-end cycle time from accepted board state to verified robot move ranging from 3 to 15 s, with a 7.5 s average. That number matters because it reflects what the user experiences, not just what the image-processing notebook can do in isolation. The reason for the gap between millisecond-scale perception and multi-second gameplay is that the full loop includes motion, settling time, and post-drop verification. Earlier benchmarking on the same project reported only 8.47 ms for rotation, 3.60 ms for perspective warp, and 0.76 ms for the deployed 5×5 Gaussian stage on the Pi, so the visible latency is dominated by mechanics and confirmation rather than by image processing itself.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: Figure 5 shows the system-level proof sequence used in the final demo story. A human move is first accepted into the trusted state, the robot then plans its response, and the next accepted frame confirms the post-drop board. This matters because it demonstrates the actual closed loop, not just a sequence of isolated screenshots. The same final course materials also recorded 31/31 passed core checks spanning win detection, gravity-correct updates, validator rules, minimax edge cases, and simulator progressions. That result matters because it isolates the logic layer from the hardware layer.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The reason it strengthens the overall project is that it shows the state machine and planner were stable before mechanical uncertainty entered the loop, even though it should not be read as a counted benchmark of full physical games.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: The strongest outcome of this project is not any one classifier score or any one demo video. It is the fact that the robot treats both perception and actuation as potentially fallible and therefore refuses to advance its internal state without evidence. The trusted-state validator protects the planner from impossible boards, and the post-drop re-check protects the planner from believing a move happened when the hardware actually missed. In a physical robot, that distinction is more valuable than a marginal gain in standalone classifier accuracy. The three-mode comparison also leads to a practical, not ideological, conclusion.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: HSV is not universally better than learning-based methods, but it is the right default for the tested setup because its assumptions match the data that was actually collected: a fixed camera, a known blue frame, red and yellow tokens, and controlled indoor lighting. The ML and Auto modes remain useful because they show an extensible path beyond thresholding, but the current evidence does not justify displacing HSV as the primary runtime mode. The main limitation is the mechanical dispenser, especially the time-based carriage. The inner columns prove that the concept works, but the outer-column degradation shows that the current actuation path is not yet uniformly reliable across the full board width.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: A carriage encoder or homing feedback would attack the dominant failure directly. This is the highest-leverage hardware improvement because it addresses the part of the loop that the final data identifies as the actual bottleneck. The second major limitation is environmental robustness. The final tests were run with a fixed mounting geometry, a stable indoor setup, and the blue board clearly separated from the background. That is a fair engineering boundary for a course robot, but it is not evidence of universal deployment robustness. Lighting shifts, glare, and domain changes remain real limits, especially for the fixed-threshold HSV path and the small-data ML path. The current system therefore demonstrates successful integrated operation under the tested conditions, not guaranteed generalization to arbitrary rooms or camera placements.

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: This paper documented a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which board reading, trusted-state acceptance, move planning, token placement, and camera-based re-verification form one closed loop. The final results support four clear conclusions: the project achieved representative end-to-end integrated demonstrations, HSV was the strongest practical vision mode under the tested setup, mechanical drop reliability was the dominant real-world bottleneck, and the final system remained limited by lighting shift and open-loop carriage mechanics. The key lesson is therefore architectural as much as algorithmic. A modest mechatronics system becomes far more trustworthy when it treats camera inference and physical execution as hypotheses to be checked, not as facts to be assumed. That lesson generalizes beyond Connect-4 and is the main reason this project reaches a stronger final quality bar than a checklist-driven pipeline demo.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot: Supplementary Material Andrew Abdelmalak, Daniel Boules, David Girgis, Kirolous Kirolous, Samir Yacoub, and Youssef Salama Dept. of Mechatronics Engineering, German University in Cairo Cairo, Egypt Abstract—This document accompanies our paper, Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot: Closed-Loop Game-State Extraction and Verified Token Placement. It collects the material the paper leaves out: how the design developed from a literature review to the final build, the parts and costs of the earlier and final designs, the dispenser’s actuation sequence, per-operation timing on the Raspberry Pi, and detailed drop, timing, and scenario results.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: All numbers come from the reports we wrote during the project. Where the final code uses different values, the text gives the code’s values. I. HOW THE DESIGN DEVELOPED A. Literature Review We began by surveying three research threads that a vision-guided Connect-4 robot depends on: board detection and game-state extraction [1], [2], token colour segmentation under changing light [3], [4], and manipulators for board games [5]. The paper’s related-work section discusses these works. The review fixed one design constraint early. Connect-4 tokens fall under gravity once released above a column, so the robot needs no grasping motion, only repeatable placement along one horizontal axis with an error below half the column pitch, about 20 mm on a standard board.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: B. Image Pipeline and First Hardware Next, we built and tested each image operation on a sample board photo: rotation and perspective warp, each with nearestneighbour and bilinear interpolation; a brightness shift and contrast scaling, each checked with histograms; and Gaussian smoothing at 3×3, 5×5, and 7×7 against a box filter. Bilinear interpolation removed the jagged cell boundaries that nearestneighbour sampling produced. The repository’s image-pipeline notebook reproduces these comparisons. Two image features were defined to drive the actuator: the mean board brightness and the board’s rotation angle. On our test image the mean brightness was 91.19, which mapped to a motor speed of about 35% PWM duty.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: An Arduino prototype turned a servo from these two values; it is in the repository as arduino/servo_prototype. The first mechanism, modelled in SolidWorks, held a stack of tokens over a slide. ADC motor with an end effector pushed out the bottom token, and a servo-driven gate covered the columns that the token should pass, so that it slid into the target column. The planned electronics drove NEMA 17 stepper motors through L298N drivers. Table I lists the cost of this design. Circuit simulated in Proteus for the closed-loop stage: the Arduino Uno, two L298N H-bridge modules for the motors, a 12 V supply, and the servo for the column gate.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: C. Closed-Loop Integration We then connected the stages into one loop: the Raspberry Pi reads the board, plans a move, and sends the column to the Arduino over USB serial, and a Flask dashboard shows the live camera streams. This version still used the stepper motors and the servo gate. D. Final Build Closed-loop testing showed that a simpler split was more repeatable: a time-based carriage driven by a TT geared DC motor, and an encoder-coupled DC motor that releases exactly one token per turn of its disk. The carriage is a rod inside an open rail along the top of the board; it slides out from the storage end and covers the holes before the target column, so the released token rolls along the rail by gravity and drops through the first open hole.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: The servo and the steppers were removed. The final build cost 6,100 EGP (Table I). II. ACTUATION SEQUENCE The Pi sends one ASCII digit, ‘1’ to ‘7’, at 9600 baud. The repository’s arduino/dispenser/dispenser.ino is rebuilt from this sequence, because the original file was not kept. passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: The dispenser’s per-move sequence, as pseudocode of the sketch that ran in the demonstrations. pushes the bottom token out of the storage tube. Hard braking drives both H-bridge inputs high for 100 ms before disabling the channel; it removed coasting and was a key source of repeatable positioning. Table II lists the calibrated carriage times. A. Token Drops by Column Each column received 20 drop trials; a drop succeeded when the token landed in the commanded column (Table IV). The misses on the outer columns come from drift in the time-based carriage positioning.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: B. End-to-End Time End-to-end time runs from the moment the column command is issued to the moment the camera verifies the new token in the commanded column. It ranged from 3.0 s at best to 15.0 s at worst, with an average of 7.5 s. The average case breaks down roughly as: 0.05 s vision, 0.01 s validation, 0.95 s minimax, 0.9 s carriage stroke out (middle columns), 2.0 s carriage pause, 0.7 s magazine release, 0.5 s settle, 0.9 s carriage stroke back, and 1.5 s verification. Moves to the home column skip both carriage strokes and finish in about 3 s; the slowest moves combine a far-column stroke with a verification retry after a borderline detection.

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: C. Closed-Loop Scenarios Mid-game states. Each of the 12 predefined simulator states was set up on the board, captured by the camera, and compared with the expected board. The validator accepted every legal change and rejected every injected illegal one, such as a chip floating two rows above the lowest empty row. • Glare. A handheld light was swept across the board mid-game. The corner smoothing kept the warp stable; one or two frames gave spurious cell readings, and the validator rejected them without touching the trusted board. Clean readings returned within 1 to 2 frames after the light moved away. •

passages.title: Supplement
passages.text: III. TIMING ON THE RASPBERRY P I Each pipeline operation was timed over 100 iterations on the Pi and on a laptop for reference (Table III). Both produce bitfor-bit identical images; the Pi is limited in throughput only. The brightness and contrast settings in the table are the ones used for this benchmark; the robot’s code applies a brightness shift of +20 and a contrast gain of 1.3. Twenty column-7 commands were sent in a row from a fresh board. Seventeen tokens landed in column 7 and three slipped into column 6; the camera check caught all three, and the robot stopped in its error state until reset.
